newsitem.title: GERMANY: Buba's Jochimsen sees EMU prospects at risk.
newsitem.headline: Buba's Jochimsen sees EMU prospects at risk.

text.p: Bundesbank council member Reimut Jochimsen warned that prospects for European monetary union (EMU) were being threatened by a lack of political integration and by a fundamental dissent between France and Germany.

Jochimsen told reporters at a dinner on Wednesday evening that monetary union "hangs in the balance" because the Amsterdam summit of EU leaders last week failed to provide a solid basis for further political integration.
"I'm not against the euro. It can be a good thing if the political and economic preconditions are right. They are not at present," Jochimsen said.
EU leaders in Amsterdam agreed on the "lowest common denominator" without mapping a clear path for integration or outlining a political vision for Europe, Jochimsen said.

They failed to agree on the issue of majority voting, on the future distribution of votes in the Council of Ministers, on reducing the size of the Commission and on improving EU coordination on foreign and defence policy, he said.

He added that the stability and growth pact designed to ensure budget discipline after monetary union did not guarantee the success of the euro. The pact lacked teeth in practice and was no substitute for the absence of political coherence and of confidence by EU states in each other.

Jochimsen also warned that France and Germany urgently needed to resolve fundamental differences regarding French calls for a political counterweight to the European Central Bank and for EU-wide policies to create jobs.

That dissent had placed a "heavy burden" on European integration, Jochimsen said. He supported the German view that job creation measures were a matter for national governments and that there could be no "European solution to unemployment."
The Amsterdam summit last week approved the pact together with a resolution on boosting employment and growth, included at French insistence.

Jochimsen added he was concerned that debate in the coming months would focus on speculation the Maastricht Treaty's convergence criteria would be softened because of fears France no longer wanted to, and Germany no longer could, fulfil them strictly.
"I am very worried that the commitment to fiscal discipline before and after monetary union has not really been accepted," Jochimsen said.
He reiterated that the EU should stick to the scheduled January 1, 1999 start date for EMU even if only a small group were able to qualify.

But asked if he saw a danger of a postponement, Jochimsen said, "Yes, very much so, very much so." He added that a postponement would not necessarily lead to a sustained appreciation of the mark on foreign exchanges.
Jochimsen also said that the choice of EMU members should depend more on their ability to maintain lasting fiscal discipline than on exact adherence to the deficit and debt reference levels.
The Maastricht Treaty states that a nation's budget deficit must not exceed three percent of its gross domestic product and its public debt must not exceed 60 percent.
But Jochimsen said the Treaty gave "stability-oriented leeway" for interpretation, allowing an overshoot of the reference levels in certain circumstances.
"The debate about decimal points is not the real issue, long-term adherence is," Jochimsen said.
